title: Already rewarded
hook: have I done something for the common good? then I've been rewarded (Meditations 11.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Marcus, and the reasoning soul that gathers its own fruit. Your line was gather your own harvest.

Somewhere in most of us there's a receipt book. Drove her to the airport: one slip. Covered his shift: another. Remembered the birthday, listened for an hour on the phone, lent the ladder and got it back with a dent. Nobody asked us to keep it. We keep it anyway, and every slip says the same thing underneath: you owe me. Marcus wrote a short note in book eleven that closes the book before the first slip is written.
screen: `A RECEIPT BOOK IN YOUR HEAD.` → `EVERY SLIP SAYS: YOU OWE ME.` → `ALREADY REWARDED.`

segments.voice: First, the note. Have I done something for the common good? Marcus asks. Then I've been rewarded. Keep this always at hand, he adds, and never stop. Second, why it's already paid. In book nine he put it sharply: wanting a return for a kindness is like an eye demanding a fee for seeing, or feet for walking. Seeing is what an eye is for. For Marcus, working with and for others is what a person is for, so the doing is the payment. Third, one letter. In book seven he plays on two Greek words that differ by a single letter. Melos means a limb, like an arm or a hand. Meros means a part, a piece, like one brick in a pile. Think of yourself as only a part of humankind, he says, and you don't yet love people from the heart; you do good because it's proper, as a duty. Think of yourself as a limb of the one body, and doing good becomes doing good to yourself. A hand doesn't send the arm an invoice. Fourth, why it's freeing. If the reward is in the doing, no one can cheat you or ignore you out of it. The account is settled the moment you act. Thanks is still welcome. You just aren't waiting for it.
screen: `DONE FOR THE COMMON GOOD? PAID.` · `AN EYE DOESN'T CHARGE FOR SEEING.` · `A LIMB, NOT JUST A PART.` · `NO ACCOUNT TO KEEP.` · then, large: `ALREADY REWARDED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one slip from your own receipt book, a favor you're still quietly waiting to have repaid. Picture yourself not as a separate piece but as one hand on a body that includes that person too, and let the slip go, just for now.
Already rewarded. Marcus's note: have I done something for the common good? Then I've been rewarded already. Today's word.
Your line: no invoice. The good you did was paid for the moment you did it. That's day six hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: People who take this note seriously often do small, unannounced things for shared spaces and neighbors, and treat the doing itself as the point rather than waiting for thanks.

original.note: Greek: a limb. In 7.13 Marcus tells himself to be a limb of humankind, not a mere part (μέρος).

trapdoor: what you thought: virtue is its own reward, a cliché.
what it means: acting for the common good is what we're made for, so the doing pays in full, and you can stop keeping the account.
what a scholar hears: Marcus makes the point three ways across the book: the note in 11.4, the eye that asks no fee in 9.42, and in 7.13 the one-letter pun on melos, limb, and meros, part.

notes: 11.4 paraphrased (Long: 'Have I done something for the general interest? Well then I have had my reward. Let this always be present to thy mind, and never stop doing such good.'). Confirm.

7.13 paraphrased (Long: if thou sayest that thou art a part, thou dost not yet love men from thy heart; beneficence does not yet delight thee for its own sake; thou doest it as a thing of propriety, not as doing good to thyself). Confirm the melos/meros wordplay (μέλος vs μέρος) and the paraphrase.
